## Core Overview
This document provides a foundational overview of Statistics and Probability, designed for undergraduate students. The primary themes include data classification, methods of data presentation (tabular and graphical), measures of central tendency, measures of dispersion, and the fundamental principles of probability theory.

## Key Concepts & Formulas

### Data and Variables
- Variable: A characteristic that varies between elements (e.g., income, height).
- Types of Variables:
    - Quantitative: Represents numerical quantity (Discrete: countable integers; Continuous: any numerical value over an interval).
    - Qualitative (Categorical): Non-numeric categories (e.g., gender, color).

### Data Presentation
- Tabular Methods: Frequency distributions, cumulative, relative, and percentage frequency distributions.
- Graphical Methods: Histograms, frequency polygons, frequency curves, bar charts, and pie charts.
- Stem-and-Leaf Display: A method for organizing data by separating leading digits (stems) from trailing digits (leaves).

### Measures of Central Tendency
- Arithmetic Mean: Sum of all values divided by the number of values.
    - Population Mean (mu): Sum(x_i) / N
    - Sample Mean (x-bar): Sum(x_i) / n
- Geometric Mean (G.M): Nth root of the product of N values. Also calculated as the antilog of the arithmetic mean of the logs of the values.
- Harmonic Mean (H.M): N / Sum(1 / x_i).
- Median: The middle value of an ordered data set.
- Mode: The value that occurs most frequently in a data set.

### Measures of Dispersion
- Absolute Measures: Range, Mean Deviation, Variance, Standard Deviation.
- Relative Measures: Coefficient of Range, Coefficient of Mean Deviation, Coefficient of Variation.

### Probability Theory
- Sample Space (S): The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.
- Event: A subset of the sample space.
- Addition Law: P(A or B) = P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
- Conditional Probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
- Multiplication Rule: P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B | A).

## Exam Takeaways
- Understand the distinction between discrete and continuous variables, as this dictates the choice of graphical representation.
- Memorize the formulas for Mean, Median, and Mode, and be prepared to calculate them from raw data.
- Know the properties of a "good" measure of central tendency (e.g., rigidly defined, based on all values, not affected by extreme values).
- Master the Addition and Multiplication rules of probability, as these are frequently tested in word problems involving dice, cards, and selection experiments.
- Be able to construct a frequency distribution and a stem-and-leaf plot from a provided set of numbers.
